vars.label: Health center sites (permanent)
vars.ref: HRSA Data Warehouse: Health Center Service Delivery and Look-Alike Sites
vars.definition: Permanent sites where a health center that holds a federal grant (a Federally Qualified Health Center, FQHC) or a look-alike designation delivers care, in the municipality HRSA gives for the site. HRSA lists a site only while its organization holds the grant or the look-alike status and the site is open. Administrative-only buildings, mobile vans and seasonal sites are not counted here. A site is a place, not an organization (one organization can run many) and says nothing about hours, services or how many people it serves. A municipality with none shows 0: HRSA lists no site there.

vars.label: Health center mobile vans
vars.ref: HRSA Data Warehouse: Health Center Service Delivery and Look-Alike Sites
vars.definition: Mobile vans that HRSA lists as service delivery sites of a health center, in the municipality HRSA gives for the van. A van can serve other municipalities, so this shows where it is listed, not everywhere it works. A municipality with none shows 0: HRSA lists no van there.

vars.label: Primary care physicians still needed, full-time equivalents (shortage areas)
vars.ref: HRSA Data Warehouse: Health Professional Shortage Area designations, primary care
vars.definition: The number of additional primary care physicians, in full-time equivalents, that HRSA says the designated shortage area still needs to bring its ratio of people to practitioners down to the ratio HRSA works the figure out against. That is 3,000 people for each physician, the goal that HRSA's file states for these designations, so reaching it would end the designation. HRSA counts a practitioner by the time spent serving the designated population: for a low-income population, the time spent on Medicaid and sliding-fee patients (HRSA's Shortage Designation Management System manual, August 2026), so a practitioner who serves few such patients adds little or nothing. Shown for a municipality that has a designated shortage area for its low-income residents or for the whole municipality (area-level designations). No value means HRSA's file has no such designation for the municipality: it is not rated as a shortage area, which is not the same as missing data. Designations of facilities (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out. The Puerto Rico figure adds the municipal figures and leaves out the facilities, so it is a little below HRSA's own total.

vars.label: Primary care physicians in place (% of the need)
vars.ref: HRSA Data Warehouse: Health Professional Shortage Area designations, primary care
vars.definition: Of the primary care physicians that HRSA's formula says the designated shortage area needs, the share that are in place: practitioners available (full-time equivalents) divided by practitioners available plus practitioners still needed. This is HRSA's "percent of need met", worked out here for each municipality. It is not the share of people who get care. 0 means HRSA counts none serving the designated population; 100 means HRSA's formula needs no more. HRSA counts a practitioner by the time spent serving the designated population: for a low-income population, the time spent on Medicaid and sliding-fee patients (HRSA's Shortage Designation Management System manual, August 2026), so a practitioner who serves few such patients adds little or nothing. Shown for a municipality that has a designated shortage area for its low-income residents or for the whole municipality (area-level designations). No value means HRSA's file has no such designation for the municipality: it is not rated as a shortage area, which is not the same as missing data. Designations of facilities (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out.

vars.label: Primary care shortage priority score
vars.ref: HRSA Data Warehouse: Health Professional Shortage Area designations, primary care
vars.definition: HRSA's priority score for a designated primary care shortage area (HRSA scores primary care designations from 0 to 25): the higher the score, the greater the priority for placing National Health Service Corps clinicians. It is an index that HRSA builds by its own rules, not a measurement, and a municipality's score is that of its area-level designation (the highest, if it has more than one). Shown for a municipality that has a designated shortage area for its low-income residents or for the whole municipality (area-level designations). No value means HRSA's file has no such designation for the municipality: it is not rated as a shortage area, which is not the same as missing data. Designations of facilities (health centers, which HRSA designates by law, and a correctional facility) are left out. Scores are not added or averaged, so there is no value for Puerto Rico as a whole.

hrsa_sites.note: Sites of health centers that hold a federal grant (FQHC) or look-alike status, with the county of each site. The observatory publishes counts for each municipality, never the names, addresses or coordinates.

hrsa_hpsa.note: Primary care, dental health and mental health designations. The observatory publishes the area-level designations of each municipality: the priority score, the practitioners still needed and the share of need met.
